name: Ryan Anderson
current_role: Co-founder and CEO, Filevine (legal-work software, Salt Lake City)
profile: Former personal-injury trial lawyer who co-founded Bighorn Law in Las Vegas with Nate Morris, then co-founded Filevine in 2014 with Morris and engineer Jim Blake to replace the firm's spreadsheets. Filevine moved HQ to Salt Lake City in 2020 and raised a $400M all-equity round in 2025; it now pitches an AI 'Legal Operating Intelligence System'.
interesting_fact: Utah Business named him a 2026 Leader of the Year; he credits mentorship from Ryan Smith (owner of the Utah Jazz) and Filevine's $400M 2025 round was among the largest in Utah tech history.
deep_cut_fact: Filevine began as software built in his basement for his own law firm; he says he 'knew at that moment this was going to work' when colleagues found it indispensable during a deposition. He holds a law degree from BYU and tried his last case around 2016.

public_contacts.value: The Hoffman Agency for Filevine: filevine@hoffman.com

notes: Frequent podcast guest (LawNext, Legal Talk Network) and Utah Business columnist; AI-in-regulated-industries is his current theme. Co-founder Jim Blake is deceased ('the late Jim Blake').

name: Cameron Zoub
current_role: Co-founder and Chief Growth Officer, Whop (Brooklyn, NY)
profile: Gen-Z founder who, as a teenager, built and sold sneaker bots with Steven Schwartz under the Sole Sniper name. In 2021 they and CTO Jack Sharkey launched Whop, first a marketplace for renting sneaker bots, now a platform for selling digital products, communities and courses. Whop raised a $200M Series D at a $5.1B valuation in Oct 2026.
interesting_fact: Whop's Oct 2026 Series D, led by Sequoia and Shopify Ventures, valued the company at $5.1B; Sequoia's Doug Leone said it was doing about half a billion in revenue.
deep_cut_fact: Schwartz found him on Facebook as 'a like-minded teen' to help build a bot that bought limited-edition sneakers before they sold out; the pair later sold bots under the name Sole Sniper, years before Whop.
notes: Bylines Whop blog announcements as 'Co-founder & CGO @ Whop'. Appeared on Max Tornow's podcast (Jan 2025) and 'We're Gonna Make It' (Oct 2025). Hurun's $2B valuation is outdated.

name: Gu Jie
current_role: Founder and CEO, Fourier (Fourier Intelligence), Shanghai
profile: Gu Jie (Alex Gu), a Shanghai Jiao Tong University mechanics graduate (2003) and ex-National Instruments engineer, founded Fourier in Shanghai in 2015 to make rehabilitation robots and exoskeletons. In 2019 it moved into general-purpose humanoids; its GR-1 (2023) was billed as China's first mass-produced humanoid, followed by GR-2.
interesting_fact: Fourier pivoted from rehab robotics to humanoids in 2019; GR-1 launched at the 2023 World AI Conference in Shanghai and more than 100 units had been delivered by mid-2024.
deep_cut_fact: Fourier is his second robotics company: in 2012 he founded Jinghe Robot, maker of the Flexbot rehab robot, which was acquired by QJ Rehab in 2015, the same year he started Fourier.
notes: No published press email found (search budget ran out before a dedicated press search). Speaks at WAIC and industry events; English name Alex Gu.

name: Bentzion Levinson
current_role: Founder and CEO, Heven AeroTech (formerly Heven Drones), HQ Sterling, Virginia
profile: Israeli-American founder who started Heven Drones in 2019 to build runway-independent, hydrogen-fuel-cell drones, initially working closely with Israel's Ministry of Defense. Renamed Heven AeroTech, it moved HQ to Virginia, opened a 56,000 sq ft plant in Winchester, and reached a $1B valuation on a $100M round led by IonQ in Dec 2025.
interesting_fact: Heven's Z1 is described as the only hydrogen-powered drone on the U.S. DIU 'Blue UAS Select' cleared list.
deep_cut_fact: Before founding Heven he served as an IDF combat commander; of his first new aircraft he said: 'It's amazing to get this feeling of seeing a dream come to life.'
notes: Hydrogen/energy angle fits the podcast. Strong defense focus; lead investor in unicorn round was quantum company IonQ.
